edge_case_manual_audit.explanation: The generic '1 is a monic constant polynomial' example fails in the zero ring because 1_R=0_R and the constant polynomial is zero, whose degree is undefined. The mathematically correct nonzero-polynomial leading-coefficient definition does not require a global R≠0 assumption; only the degree-zero example explicitly needs R≠0. Check source and preserve as a review-ledger item before publication.

items.origin_mathematical_context: Set theory: injectivity of an arbitrary map f:X→Y, meaning f(x)=f(y) implies x=y for all x,y in X; for structured maps this is the underlying-set condition.
items.draft_definition: A function f:X→Y is injective (one-to-one) if, for all x,x'∈X, the equality f(x)=f(x') implies x=x'. Equivalently, no two distinct elements of X have the same image.
mathematical_scope_and_edge_cases: Underlying-set injectivity makes sense for any function; it need not coincide with being a categorical monomorphism in arbitrary categories.
If X is empty the condition holds vacuously; an injective function does not need to be surjective.
items.comparison_to_prior_independent_meanings: No equality with any stored provisional meaning; it may be an ingredient of structured maps and exact sequences.

items.origin_mathematical_context: Set theory: surjective function f:X→Y whose image is the entire stated codomain Y; for module homomorphisms this is the underlying-set surjectivity of the R-linear map, independent of linearity, free domain, or choice of basis.
items.draft_term: Surjective function, including a surjective linear map
items.draft_definition: A function f:X→Y is surjective (onto) if, for every y∈Y, there exists x∈X such that f(x)=y. If f:R^n→M is R-linear, surjective means the same underlying-set condition; linearity and the free domain are additional hypotheses of that application.
mathematical_scope_and_edge_cases: When Y=∅, an existing function X→Y forces X=∅ and that empty function is onto.

For a unital module M, an R-linear surjection R^n→M exists precisely when M is generated by at most n elements, but surjectivity as a function is not the same mathematical object as a chosen generating family.
items.comparison_to_prior_independent_meanings: No exact identity with the provisional catalog; bounded linear maps are maps with an additional analytic property, not the definition of surjectivity.

items.origin_mathematical_context: Category theory: f:X→Y is an isomorphism iff there exists g:Y→X with gf=id_X and fg=id_Y; no underlying-set bijectivity is assumed.
items.draft_definition: Given objects X and Y of a category C, a morphism f:X→Y is an isomorphism if there exists a morphism g:Y→X with g∘f=1_X and f∘g=1_Y. Such a g is unique when it exists and is denoted f^{-1}.
mathematical_scope_and_edge_cases: The inverse here is a morphism and need not be an inverse function on underlying sets: an arbitrary category may have no underlying-set functor.
Every identity morphism is an isomorphism; the composite of two composable isomorphisms is an isomorphism.
Being a monomorphism and epimorphism simultaneously need not imply isomorphism in an arbitrary category.
items.comparison_to_prior_independent_meanings: Distinct from bijective functions and from a property such as connectedness in the existing provisional catalog.

items.origin_mathematical_context: Commutative algebra: scalar extension of a commutative unital k-algebra R along field extension K/k, yielding the unital K-algebra R⊗_k K with induced multiplication (r⊗a)(s⊗b)=rs⊗ab and K-scalar structure.
items.draft_term: Extension of scalars of a commutative k-algebra
items.draft_definition: Let k⊆K be a field extension and let R be a commutative unital k-algebra. The extension of scalars of R from k to K is R_K:=R⊗_k K, equipped with K-algebra structure a·(r⊗b)=r⊗ab, multiplication (r⊗a)(s⊗b)=rs⊗ab, and identity 1_R⊗1_K.
mathematical_scope_and_edge_cases: No finite-degree or separability assumption on K/k is required for the construction.
R=0 gives the zero K-algebra under conventions that allow it.
Extension of scalars need not preserve every property of R; for example a field extension can cause a non-geometrically-integral algebra to acquire zero divisors after base change.
items.comparison_to_prior_independent_meanings: Distinct from an arbitrary tensor product of modules and from bounded linear transformations in the provisional population.

items.origin_mathematical_context: Order theory: supremum sup(A) of subset A⊆S, an upper bound no greater than every other upper bound when it exists.
items.draft_definition: Let (S,≤) be a partially ordered set and A⊆S. An element u∈S is the supremum sup A if (i) a≤u for every a∈A and (ii) for every v∈S satisfying a≤v for every a∈A, one has u≤v. Such an element, if it exists, is unique.
mathematical_scope_and_edge_cases: A supremum need not belong to A.
For A=∅, every element of S is an upper bound; hence sup∅ exists exactly when S has a least element.
If A has no upper bound in S then no supremum exists in S.
items.comparison_to_prior_independent_meanings: No exact match among independent provisional means; analytic suprema of sets of norms are applications requiring codomain completeness/boundedness.

items.origin_mathematical_context: Category theory: hom-collection Hom_C(X,Y) of arrows X→Y; a preadditive category requires these collections to be sets carrying abelian group structures, without requiring all objects to form a set.
items.draft_term: Hom-collection between two objects of a category
items.draft_definition: For objects X,Y in a category C, Hom_C(X,Y) denotes the collection of all morphisms f:X→Y in C. If C is locally small, Hom_C(X,Y) is a set; an unrestricted category need not have set-sized Hom-collections under every foundational convention.
mathematical_scope_and_edge_cases: Do not assume the class of all objects is a set.
When C is preadditive, each Hom_C(X,Y) is customarily an abelian group, so the corresponding Hom is a set in ordinary set-based algebra.
Hom_C(X,Y) may be empty, and Hom_C(X,X) contains 1_X.
items.comparison_to_prior_independent_meanings: A component of ordinary category and functor definitions, not identical to either whole structure.

items.origin_mathematical_context: Polynomial algebra: a nonzero univariate polynomial f(X)=a_nX^n+⋯+a_0 over a commutative unital coefficient ring is monic if its leading coefficient a_n equals the multiplicative identity 1, including degree zero unit polynomial 1.
items.draft_definition: Let R be a commutative unital ring and f(X)∈R[X] be a nonzero polynomial of degree n. The polynomial f is monic if its leading coefficient, the coefficient of X^n, equals 1_R. Over a nonzero ring, the constant polynomial 1_R is monic of degree zero.
mathematical_scope_and_edge_cases: The zero polynomial has no degree or leading coefficient in the usual convention and is not monic by this definition.
If R is the zero ring then 1_R=0_R, so there are no nonzero polynomials. The phrase 'constant polynomial 1 is monic' must carry R≠0 (or use a separately identified source convention).
The coefficient ring need not be a field; monicity makes sense over commutative rings with 1.
items.comparison_to_prior_independent_meanings: A specialization of general polynomial-ring notation, not the polynomial ring itself.

items.origin_mathematical_context: Algebraic geometry: distinguished principal open D(f)={p∈Spec(R):f∉p} of a commutative ring's affine spectrum.
items.draft_term: Distinguished principal open subset of an affine spectrum
items.draft_definition: Let R be a commutative ring and f∈R. The distinguished (principal) open subset D(f) of Spec(R) is D(f):={p∈Spec(R) : f∉p}. It is open in the Zariski topology, being the complement of V((f)).
mathematical_scope_and_edge_cases: D(0)=∅ and D(1_R)=Spec(R), including when Spec(R) is empty.
D(fg)=D(f)∩D(g); D(f) is empty if f is nilpotent.
D(f) carries the standard affine scheme structure isomorphic to Spec(R_f) when that additional structure is considered.
items.comparison_to_prior_independent_meanings: An instance of a topologically open subset in algebraic geometry, not synonymous with a generic open subset or a ring spectrum.

items.origin_mathematical_context: Commutative algebra: product IJ of two ideals of a commutative unital ring R, generated by finite sums of pairwise products; ordinary ideal powers I^n for n≥1 by repeated ideal multiplication, and by convention I^0=R when nonnegative exponents are used.
items.draft_term: Product and nonnegative powers of ideals
items.draft_definition: For ideals I,J of a commutative ring R, their product IJ is the ideal consisting of all finite sums Σ_{k=1}^n a_k b_k with a_k∈I and b_k∈J (including the empty sum 0). Define I^n recursively for n≥1 by I^1=I and I^{n+1}=I^n I; for a unital ring, set I^0=R when using exponent zero.
mathematical_scope_and_edge_cases: I·R=I for unital commutative R, and I·0=0.
An arbitrary product of ideal elements is not by itself an ideal element unless finite sums are allowed; the generated-ideal construction matters.
Positive powers also exist in many nonunital ring conventions, while the I^0=R convention requires deliberate scope.
items.comparison_to_prior_independent_meanings: Not identical to nilpotent ideals, which are a property defined by I^n=0 for some positive n.

items.origin_mathematical_context: Commutative algebra: kernel ideal of a unital homomorphism φ:A→B of commutative rings, consisting of all a∈A mapped to 0_B; for a polynomial evaluation map it is the ideal of polynomial relations, and for a quotient-localization composite it is the inverse image of zero in the target ring.
items.draft_term: Kernel ideal of a commutative ring homomorphism
items.draft_definition: For a ring homomorphism φ:A→B between commutative rings, its kernel is ker φ:={a∈A:φ(a)=0_B}. This is an ideal of A. If φ is surjective, the first isomorphism theorem supplies a canonical ring isomorphism A/ker φ ≅ B.
mathematical_scope_and_edge_cases: The kernel can be A when B is the zero ring and zero rings/unital maps are permitted.
If φ is a polynomial evaluation map, the kernel describes polynomial relations satisfied by the chosen images.
A kernel ideal differs in type from a kernel of an arbitrary function; for an underlying set map the preimage of {0_B} need not be an ideal unless the map is algebraic.
items.comparison_to_prior_independent_meanings: A particular algebraic use of set-theoretic preimage, and a component prerequisite of quotient ring constructions.

items.origin_candidate_query: direct sum ⊕_i M_i of a family of modules
items.origin_mathematical_context: Module theory: direct sum ⊕_{i∈I} M_i of left R-modules, the module of families (m_i) of finite support with componentwise addition and scalar multiplication, distinct from their unrestricted product.
items.draft_term: Direct sum of an indexed family of left modules
items.draft_definition: Let (M_i)_{i∈I} be a family of left modules over the same ring R. Their direct sum ⊕_{i∈I}M_i consists of all tuples (m_i)∈∏_{i∈I}M_i for which the set {i∈I:m_i≠0} is finite, with componentwise addition and scalar multiplication.
mathematical_scope_and_edge_cases: For I=∅ the direct sum is the zero module.
For finite I the direct sum equals the direct product in the canonical tuple model; for infinite I with infinitely many nonzero summands, direct sum is generally a proper submodule of the product.
The direct sum of copies of R is free with its standard indexed basis over a unital R, while direct sum of general modules need not be free.
items.comparison_to_prior_independent_meanings: A component of the free-module construction (when every M_i=R), not the same as an arbitrary free module with a chosen basis.
